newsitem.title: USA: Peru Brady deal may close in February - US sources.
newsitem.headline: Peru Brady deal may close in February - US sources.

text.p: Peru is putting the finishing touches on its protracted debt restructuring deal and the closing could come before the end of February, U.S. investment banking sources said.
Peru's Economy Minister Jorge Camet is in Washington to work out final details on loan support with multilateral lenders, according to the sources.

Peru needs to secure $230 million to $240 million from each of three lenders -- the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund and the InterAmerican Development Bank -- in addition to putting $550 million of its own funds to back up the deal, said Jaime Valdivia Hernandez, vice president of emerging markets research at Morgan Stanley.
One of the wrinkles to be smoothed out with the World Bank is the status of a structure adjustment loan to fund the liabilities of Peru's pension reform and to support the debt restructuring.
"We believe the fund will be released," Valdivia said, referring to the loan.
The actual closing of the debt restructuring would come 35 days after the agreement is reached, he said.

Karim Abdel-Motaal, an analyst at J.P. Morgan Securities, expected Camet and his contingent of advisers to smooth out the final details with the lenders, and considered February 28 as a realistic target for the closing.
"They are so far into the process," he said. "I don't think there's (any) turning back."

The hostage crisis that began on December 17 when the rebel group Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) stormed the Japanese Embassy has had only marginal impact on the debt restructuring schedule, he said.
The rebels complained that the government sold out to the foreigners, but the population overwhelmingly stood by President Alberto Fujimori's tough stance in handling the crisis, he said.

Peru's restructured loans trading on a "when-issued" basis largely recovered from the initial shock at the outbreak of the hostage crisis and could rise further at the final closing of the Brady deal, market sources said.
At 1200 EST/1700 GMT, Peru PDI W/I PEPDI=RR rose 1/2 to 61-1/8 and Peru FLIRB W/I PEFLIRB=RR gained 3/8 to 55-3/4.
The market currently favored the collateralized FLIRB to the uncollateralized PDI, said Vardivia, who expect the PDI to rise to 63-1/2 and FLIB to 56-1/2 by the close of the deal.

U.S. analysts agree that Peru's economy growth rate would accelerate in 1997 to about 5 percent, but some caution that the rise must be viewed against the background of an estimated 2.3 to 2.4 percent growth rate in 1996.
"Outside the fishing sector, the (Peruvian) economy is still sluggish," said Raphael del la Fuente, a Latin America economist at Paribas Securities.

Despite the effort to diversify, Peru's economy is heavily dependent on commodities exports, he said, noting that the projected buildup in world copper stocks does not bode well for Peru's copper export revenues.
And Fujimori's government, under criticism for a tight fiscal policy, would face the challenge of charting a path of growth without rekindling inflation, he said.
